item.title: US Electronic Spy Agency Suffers Classified Network Outage
item.description: The National Security Agency is suffering an outage of a classified computer network it uses for internal communications and other daily work functions, according to a US official and another person familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- The National Security Agency is suffering an outage of a classified computer network it uses for internal communications and other daily work functions, according to a US official and another person familiar with the matter.The network, known as NSA Net, has been down since at least early Tuesday morning, said the person, who spoke on the condition that they not be identified because they were not authorized to discuss the matter. Some staff of the electronic spying agency have been unable to access their workplace systems, the person said, and the issue led the NSA to tell some staff to delay their arrival at the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, the person said.The US official said the outage occurred during scheduled routine maintenance and that the agency was still able to conduct its mission critical functions. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss agency operations, said the NSA systems have multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.The NSA didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment. The outage was earlier reported by CNN.A series of technology failures have brought down critical systems that disrupted operations around the world in recent weeks. A technical glitch at JPMorgan Chase & Co. on Monday caused some customers’ transactions to take longer to process. The issue wasn’t related to a cybersecurity event, the bank said, but tied to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems. United Airlines also said on Monday a technology issue impacted its departing flights, and that the problem was traced to equipment problems involving the agency’s aging communications infrastructure. Microsoft Corp.’s productivity software was hobbled for roughly 24 hours last week after a bug caused a system malfunction during an otherwise routine rerouting of user traffic on Nov. 11. In yet another issue, US air traffic was snarled over the weekend after a problem arose when a government contractor was trying to replace outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas. US Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC before the NSA issue was reported that the recent technology failures weren’t the result of a cyberattack. (Updates with details on cause of outage in third paragraph.)More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: China’s export engine faces a reality check as domestic demand falters: Can overseas markets sustain its growth?
item.description: China's export-led growth model faces mounting pressure as weak domestic consumption, slowing factory output and a prolonged property crisis expose vulnerabilities. While AI-driven exports support growth, October data highlight the widening gap between manufacturing strength and household spending.
item.dc:creator: Bhanu Pratap
item.content:encoded: China's export-led growth model is facing a reality check as weak domestic consumption, slowing industrial production and a prolonged property crisis expose vulnerabilities in the world's second-largest economy. While strong overseas demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related products has helped sustain growth, October's economic data highlight the widening gap between China's manufacturing strength and its struggling domestic economy. The country's industrial output grew 4.8% year-on-year in October, down from 5.5% in September and below the 5.3% forecast by economists polled by Reuters. Retail sales rose just 0.4%, compared with 1.1% in September and against expectations of 0.8%. The figures raise a crucial question for Beijing: can overseas markets continue to support growth while household spending and domestic investment remain subdued? AI exports cushion China's economic slowdown Strong global demand for AI infrastructure, semiconductors and other high-tech products has emerged as an important growth driver for China. Overseas demand for technology products and automobiles helped the economy recover from a second-quarter slowdown, with gross domestic product expanding 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, Reuters reported. China's October exports also remained strong, supported by the global AI infrastructure investment boom. However, the resilience of external trade contrasts with weakening domestic indicators, exposing an increasingly uneven recovery. The imbalance could deepen as high-tech manufacturing accounts for a growing share of industrial growth, while traditional industries and consumer-facing sectors struggle with weak demand. China's official data showed that high-end and intelligent manufacturing contributed more than half of industrial output growth in the first 10 months of 2026.This suggests that the export boom is helping sustain economic activity without necessarily generating a broad-based recovery in domestic demand.Weak consumption and property crisis weigh on recoveryDomestic demand remains a major concern for Chinese policymakers. A sluggish labour market, uncertainty over future incomes and falling property prices have weakened consumer confidence, limiting household spending despite major shopping events such as the National Day holiday and Singles Day festival.Services retail sales grew 4.9% in the first 10 months of 2026, marginally slower than the 5% recorded in the first nine months, according to China's National Bureau of Statistics (NBS)."The persistently soft consumer confidence remains the main issue preventing a consumption recovery, and a more effective policy push must address this," Lynn Song, ING's chief economist for Greater China, told Reuters.The property downturn is adding to the pressure. Property investment fell 21.6% year-on-year in January-October, while new home prices declined further in October. Fixed-asset investment also contracted 8.1% during the first 10 months, worsening from a 7.2% decline in January-September, as per the report.The figures suggest that efforts to revive investment through infrastructure spending and cheaper credit have yet to deliver a meaningful recovery.Can exports sustain China's growth?China's dependence on overseas demand also leaves its economy exposed to trade restrictions, geopolitical tensions and any slowdown in global technology investment.An official factory activity survey showed that manufacturers reported weaker conditions in new orders and new export orders in October compared with September. This raises questions about whether the export momentum can be sustained even as domestic demand remains weak.Strong exports could also reduce the immediate pressure on Beijing to introduce deeper measures to revive consumption. However, relying on overseas markets cannot indefinitely compensate for weak household spending and investment.Despite calls for additional support, economists do not expect major stimulus measures before the end of 2026.
